title: Day Length Calculator: Hours of Daylight
description: Compute hours of daylight for any place and date with the Day Length Calculator — solstice extremes, polar day and night included. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, London gets 16 hours 39 minutes of daylight on 21 June 2026 and just 7 hours 50 minutes on 21 December (computed) — the same city living two different lives half a year apart.
quick_answer: The Day Length Calculator computes the hours of daylight between sunrise and sunset for any place and date, including polar cases where the answer is honestly zero or twenty-four. Enter a location and date and read the day's length — for gardens, trips and feeling the seasons in numbers.

use_cases.title: Chasing or fleeing the midnight sun

body.t: North of the Arctic Circle the calculator returns 24 hours in season — the fact behind the trip, computed for your exact dates rather than a brochure's 'summer'.

Computed for New York: 15 hours 06 minutes on 21 June 2026 (sunrise 05:24, sunset 20:30) against 9 hours 15 minutes on 21 December (07:16–16:31). Six hours of swing — the whole difference between a summer evening and a winter commute in the dark, twice.

On the equator every day of the year is about 12 hours 7 minutes — not exactly 12, because the sunrise convention counts the Sun's upper limb with refraction. The boring line on the graph is a subtlety wearing a disguise.

popular_table.intro: Standard solar algorithm, 2026 solstice dates — the year's two extremes by latitude.
popular_table.note: Day length is sunrise-to-sunset on the standard horizon. Twilight adds usable light at both ends — civil twilight alone can add an hour a day at high latitudes in summer.

faq: Sunrise to sunset, using the standard convention: the Sun's upper edge at the horizon, with average atmospheric refraction included (−0.83°). It is the almanac definition, not the moment the sky first brightens.
Why is the equinox day not exactly 12 hours?

The same convention: limb-plus-refraction buys a few extra minutes, and the equinox itself rarely falls on the date at your longitude. Most places see their true 12-hour day a few days off the equinox — the 'equilux'.
How fast does day length change?

Fastest at the equinoxes — around 2–3 minutes a day at mid-latitudes, more toward the poles — and not at all at the solstices, where the curve flattens. September steals daylight faster than December ever did.
Yes, slightly: a higher horizon view sees the Sun earlier and later — roughly a few minutes per 1,000 m in open country. Mountains on the horizon take back with interest what altitude gives.
What about places inside the polar circles?

In season the answer is the honest extreme: 24 hours (the Sun never sets) or 0 (it never rises). The calculator reports those rather than failing — they are the correct answers for real dates and towns.
Daylight saving — does it change day length?
No. Clock labels move an hour between morning and evening; the sunrise-to-sunset total is untouched. The base FAQ on this page says it plainly because everyone asks once.
Can I get a whole year for one place?

Day-by-day queries build the picture; the pattern is a smooth annual wave peaking at your summer solstice. Gardeners and photographers often chart the year around a few anchor dates from this calculator.
Why do sunrise and sunset not balance around noon?

Solar noon is rarely clock noon — longitude within the time zone and the equation of time shift it. Day length only counts the span; where the span sits in the clock day is the Sunrise Sunset Calculator's story.
